function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format [username, password].

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
It looks like you’re looking for help getting started with the **Open‑Meteo** API call that’s exposed through our custom `requests_get` helper. Below is a short “quick start” guide plus some pointers to deeper documentation so you’ll know exactly how to build your first query.

---

### Quick Start – One‑liner Example

```python
from my_toolbox import functions   # <-- adjust based on actual module path

response = functions.requests_get(
    url="https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast",
    params={
        "latitude": 40.7128,      # New York City lat
        "longitude": -74.0060,    # NYC lon
        "hourly": ["temperature_2m", "windspeed_10m"],
        "timezone": "America/New_York"
    }
)

print(response.json())          # Pretty‑printed JSON payload
```

> *What happens here?*  
> • The helper builds an HTTP GET request to the Open‑Meteo forecast endpoint.  
> • It automatically sets standard headers (`Content-Type`, `Accept`).  
> • You pass all required query parameters inside the `params` dict.  

If everything goes well, `response.json()` will contain a dictionary similar to:

```json
{
  "hourly_units": {
    "time": "iso8601",
    "temperature_2m": "°C",
    "windspeed_10m": "km/h"
  },
  "hourly": {
    "time": [...],
    "temperature_2m": [...],
    "windspeed_10m": [...]
  }
}
```

---

### Step‑by‑Step Breakdown

| Step | What to Do | Why |
|------|------------|-----|
| **1️⃣ Import the helper** | `from my_toolbox import functions` | Makes the `requests_get` callable. Replace `my_toolbox` with whatever package/module actually contains the wrapper. |
| **2️⃣ Pick a target endpoint** | Use `"https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast"` for current forecasts. Other endpoints exist—see below. | Different services return different data shapes. |
| **3️⃣ Build the `params` dict** | Include mandatory fields such as `latitude`, `longitude`. Add optional ones like `elevation`, `daily`, `hourly`, etc., depending on your needs. | These become part of the query string (`?...`) sent over HTTP. |
| **4️⃣ Call the function** | Pass `url=` + `params=...`; other keyword args stay defaults unless you have special requirements (proxy, auth, timeout). | Executes the network round‑trip. |
| **5️⃣ Inspect the result** | Usually `.json()`, `.text`, or `.status_code`. Handle errors gracefully. | Gives you access to the raw API output. |

---

### Where to Find More Detailed Instructions?

| Resource | Description | Link |
|----------|-------------|------|
| **Open‑Meteo Docs** | Official reference for available endpoints, parameter lists, units, and examples. | <https://open-meteo.com/en/docs> |
| **Python Requests Library** | Underlying HTTP mechanics behind the helper. Useful if you ever need to tweak things beyond the wrapper. | <https://docs.python-requests.org/> |
| **API Playground / Postman Collection** | Test queries manually without writing code. Handy for exploring new parameters. | Many sites host collections; search “Open‑Meteo Postman”. |
| **GitHub Repository** | Source code for the helper itself (if public), often includes README with usage notes. | Search GitHub for repo containing `functions.requests_get`. |
| **Stack Overflow & Community Forums** | Real‑world Q&A around common pitfalls (rate limits, missing data, timezone quirks). | <https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/open-meteo> |

---

#### Common Gotchas

| Issue | Fix |
|-------|-----|
| **Missing `hourly/daily` keys** | Some endpoints require specifying at least one variable list. For instance, add `"hourly": ["temperature_2m"]`. |
| **Timezone handling** | Without `timezone`, results default to UTC. Specify e.g., `"timezone": "Europe/London"`. |
| **Rate limiting** | Keep track of calls per minute/hour; throttle accordingly. |
| **Elevation vs. No scaling** | By default `elevation=None` disables downscaling. Set numeric values when you need precise altitude adjustments. |

---

Feel free to drop me a follow‑up if you hit a specific error message or need help tailoring the query to a particular dataset!
